title: Bidirectional A* in Reykjavík: Find the Fast Route!
description: Watch Bidirectional A* slice through Reykjavík’s real street graph to meet in the middle and drastically cut search effort. The visualization shows how forward and backward A* frontiers collaborate to reach the destination efficiently.
ig_caption:
🗺️✨ Reykjavík’s streets look calm—until Bidirectional A* starts searching.

🚦 With **Bidirectional A***, we run two coordinated A* searches: one from the **start** and one from the **goal** on the same **road-network graph** (nodes = intersections, edges = street segments). Each side uses an **admissible heuristic** (e.g., straight-line / great-circle distance) to guide expansion, and the algorithm stops when the frontiers **meet**, producing an efficient path with far fewer explored nodes than a single-direction search.

📍 On real maps (like Reykjavík’s Miðborg grid and coastal connectors), this becomes a graph-theory race: **frontier growth**, **priority-queue ordering by f(n)=g(n)+h(n)**, and a clean convergence condition when a node discovered from both directions matches. ⚙️🧠

🎥 Want me to visualize how changing the heuristic affects explored states and runtime? Drop a 🧠 in the comments and follow for more real-map algorithm reels!
fb_caption:
Reykjavík (Miðborg) in motion! 🌍🚦

Bidirectional A* is a graph search method that runs A* from both the start and the goal, letting the two search waves meet in the middle. That “meet-in-the-middle” strategy often reduces the number of explored intersections on real street maps—share this with a friend who loves algorithms and ask: should we use great-circle distance or a faster heuristic for colder climates? ❄️
